title: Genesis 35:16–29
context: From Bethel the family travels toward Ephrath; Rachel dies in hard labor after naming Ben-oni, whom Jacob calls Benjamin, and she is buried on the way to Bethlehem. Israel camps beyond the tower of Eder; Reuben lies with Bilhah; the twelve sons are listed. Jacob reaches Isaac at Hebron, and Isaac dies at 180, gathered to his people—buried by Esau and Jacob.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on Rachel’s death, Benjamin, and Isaac gathered to his people, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: But Jacob because he would not renew the sorrowful remembrance of his mother's death every time he called his son by name, changed his name, and called him Benjamin, the son of my right hand—That is, very dear to me; set on my right hand for a right hand blessing; the support of my age, like the staff in my right hand. Jacob buried her near the place where she died.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 35:18)

reformed.quote: We know that the ancients were very desirous of offspring, especially of male offspring. Since Rachel therefore does not accept this kind of consolation when offered, we infer that she was completely oppressed with pain. She therefore died in agonies, thinking of nothing but her sad childbirth and her own sorrows: from the feeling of which she gave a name to her son; but Jacob afterwards corrected the error.

verses.text: They traveled from Bethel. There was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and Rachel travailed. She had hard labor.
verses.arminianNotes:
The road from Bethel is not ease: still short of Ephrath, Rachel’s labor is hard. Obedience and pain can share a mile.

God’s enabling presence in flight and return does not cancel creaturely suffering. Rachel’s struggle is true; grace does not make her a prop.
verses.reformedNotes:
Promise-road and hard labor arrive together. Providence is not a cushion; it is God’s rule in the pain.

The line that will include Benjamin is being kept even here. God does not step out of the story because the labor is hard.

verses.text: When she was in hard labor, the midwife said to her, “Don’t be afraid, for now you will have another son.”
verses.arminianNotes:
At the hardest point the midwife speaks courage: do not fear, you have another son. The word is human kindness and true news.

Those in Wesley’s line hear a sincere comfort offered in crisis. Fear is met with a reason; Rachel is addressed as a person who can still receive hope.
verses.reformedNotes:
The second son of Rachel arrives under a midwife’s “Don’t be afraid.” God had opened this hope long before (30:24).

Providence uses an ordinary voice at the worst moment. The promise of another son is being kept while the mother is at the edge.

verses.text: As her soul was departing (for she died), she named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes:
As her soul departs she names him Ben-oni, son of my sorrow; the father names him Benjamin, son of the right hand. Both names tell the truth of the hour.

Rachel’s dying word is hers, not overwritten as unreal. Jacob’s rename is a responsible act of hope—sorrow acknowledged, the child not left under a name of only grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two names, one boy: sorrow and right-hand strength. The father speaks the name that will stand in Israel.

God keeps the twelfth son even as the beloved wife dies. Election of the tribes does not require that God author the pain; He weaves Benjamin into the line through a death He did not need as a scheme of cruelty.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor both names. Arminians underline Rachel’s dying agency and Jacob’s responsible hope; Reformed interpreters typically press that God still gives the tribe of the right hand without making Himself the author of the mother’s death.

verses.text: Rachel died, and was buried on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem).
verses.arminianNotes:
Rachel dies and is buried on the way—Ephrath, that is Bethlehem. The beloved is not carried home; the grave is a roadside fact.

Faith does not deny the burial. God was with this family in flight and return, and He is not absent from this grave; grief remains a human, honest response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator locates the tomb on the Bethlehem road. Promise geography now includes a grave.

Covenant faithfulness can hold a burial. The line continues toward Hebron while Rachel rests where God, not chance, has placed this milestone.

verses.text: Jacob set up a pillar on her grave. The same is the Pillar of Rachel’s grave to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jacob sets a pillar over her tomb, still known “to this day.” Love marks the place; memory is a responsible kindness.

Classical Arminians see no conflict between mourning and faith. The God who accompanied Jacob now meets him as a widower; the pillar is devotion, not unbelief.
verses.reformedNotes:
A second pillar in the chapter: one for Bethel’s speech, one for Rachel’s grave. God allows both to stand.

Providence writes a memorial into the land. The promise line will pass this pillar; God keeps Israel without erasing the cost along the road.

verses.text: Israel traveled, and spread his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel journeys on and pitches beyond the tower of Eder. Grief does not freeze the camp; he still moves as a responsible shepherd of the household.

Enabling grace for the next mile is not in doubt. The new name “Israel” is now the traveler’s name on a hard road, freely taken.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator calls him Israel on the far side of Rachel’s death. The flock moves because God still leads.

The promise does not camp forever at the tomb. Providence pushes the line on toward the next scene, tower of Eder included.

verses.text: While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.
verses.arminianNotes:
Reuben lies with Bilhah; Israel hears of it. Then, in the same verse, the sons are twelve. Sin is named as Reuben’s act, not as a necessity.

Arminians refuse to make God the author of this incestuous grab. Responsible, resistible lust wounds the household; grace had enabled a better path Reuben did not take. The twelve are still counted.
verses.reformedNotes:
The crime is Reuben’s; the hearing is Israel’s; the twelve are still God’s. Birthright will later move (49:4; 1 Chr 5:1), but the people remain.

Election of Israel does not make God the author of Reuben’s sin. Providence can judge the firstborn’s outrage and still keep twelve tribes under the promise.
verses.keyContrast: Both condemn Reuben without blaming God. Arminians underline a resistible, responsible violation Reuben chose; Reformed Christians typically emphasize that God keeps the twelve and later reorders the birthright without being the author of the sin.

verses.text: The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob’s firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
verses.arminianNotes:
Leah’s six are listed, Reuben still called firstborn. The family record is honest: status named, sin not erased from the previous verse.

Each son is a person under a sincere God, not a pawn. The household remains accountable as a family, not a mere diagram of fate.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list begins with Leah’s sons, firstborn included. God counts the tribes He will keep.

Covenant faithfulness writes names. The promise line is a people with mothers and an order—not an idea detached from these six.

verses.text: The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rachel’s two: Joseph and Benjamin. The dead mother’s sons are not dropped from the count. Gift and grief stand together.

Wesleyan Arminians receive both boys as grace to be cherished. Joseph’s later story will still require responsible choices; Benjamin is already more than a sorrow-name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Rachel’s pair complete the beloved wife’s share. The future savior of the family (Joseph) sits beside the late-born son.

God stocks the line through Rachel as through Leah. Providence has already placed Joseph in the list that famine and Egypt will need.

verses.text: The sons of Bilhah (Rachel’s servant): Dan and Naphtali.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bilhah’s sons are named after the outrage against their mother. They are not reduced to Reuben’s crime.

God sincerely regards these boys as Jacob’s sons. Status as children of a servant does not undo their belonging or their future accountability.
verses.reformedNotes:
Dan and Naphtali are counted inside Israel, not as an appendix. The promise takes in the sons of the concubine.

Election of the tribes is wider than favored wives. God keeps Bilhah’s children in the twelve without endorsing how they were conceived in the rivalry of chapter 30.

verses.text: The sons of Zilpah (Leah’s servant): Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan Aram.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zilpah’s sons complete the twelve; the narrator sums them as born in Paddan-aram. The God who was with Jacob in the far country now numbers every son as fruit of that long stay.

The verse presses a family God accompanied in sojourn. Grace attended the eastern years; the return is not an empty camp.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Paddan-aram summary folds the household into one sentence. God brought a full twelve out of the sojourn.

Covenant faithfulness counted sons in Laban’s house. The return is not empty; the promise line is already a people.

verses.text: Jacob came to Isaac his father, to Mamre, to Kiriath Arba (which is Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac lived as foreigners.
verses.arminianNotes:
The long road ends at Isaac’s tent in Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac sojourned. Reunion is gift after decades.

Jacob actually comes—responsible return to the father he fled. The God who was with him in flight now lets him stand again in the ancestral camp.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mamre, Kiriath-arba, Hebron: the old sojourning ground. God brings the heir back to the heir.

Comfort: providence closes a loop Abraham’s God opened. The promise line is physically reunited in the land, not left scattered in Paddan-aram.

verses.text: The days of Isaac were one hundred eighty years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Isaac’s days are 180 years. A long life is numbered, not mythic. Years are a created gift to receive with thanks.

Arminian interpreters read the number as God’s kindness in time, not a mechanical quota. Full years still leave the man a responsible sojourner to the end.
verses.reformedNotes:
The clock of the second patriarch is finished. One hundred eighty years under promise.

God allots the span. Covenant faithfulness includes the length of Isaac’s life; the oath does not die with his breath still coming.

verses.text: Isaac gave up the spirit and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. Esau and Jacob, his sons, buried him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Isaac dies, old and full of days, gathered to his people. Esau and Jacob bury him together—the last fraternal act in this chapter.

Application: brothers who once split over a blessing now share a grave’s work. Grace that sought peace at Peniel still invites responsible honor of a father; neither son is a puppet at the burial.
verses.reformedNotes:
Gathered to his people: the narrator’s hope-language for the patriarch. Both sons stand at the grave.

The promise does not fail when Isaac is buried. God keeps the line through Jacob while Esau also does this good; providence can use both brothers at a funeral without confusing their callings.
